summary: Registers media types for the RTP payload formats defined in the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences. Some of these formats can also be used outside RTP, so having proper media type names helps wherever they appear. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives official names to the audio and video encodings that RTP conferencing uses, so a program can say "this is PCMA audio at 8000 samples per second" in a session description. It also lists the parameters each name accepts, such as the sampling rate and the number of channels.

subtitle: The standard media type names for the audio and video encodings used in RTP conferencing sessions.

tldr.problem: The RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences, RFC 3551, defines many payload formats, but those formats had no media type names of their own. Without a name, software cannot say in a session description which encoding it is sending.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers each payload format as a subtype of the audio or video media type, such as audio/PCMA or audio/L16, and gives each registration the required and optional parameters that describe the encoding, such as the sampling rate and the number of interleaved channels.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4856 is a Proposed Standard from March 2007 that makes no technical changes to the registrations. Together with RFC 4855 it obsoletes RFC 3555, and the registrations for payload formats defined in other RFCs are left to those documents to update.

today: RFC 4856 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2007. Together with RFC 4855 it obsoletes RFC 3555, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. The registrations for the payload formats that other RFCs define are updated by those documents, not by this one.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4856 updates the media type registrations initially specified in RFC 3555 for the RTP payload formats defined in the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences, RFC 3551. They are registered as subtypes under the audio and video media types.

The document deliberately leaves out the payload formats that RFC 3551 references but that other RFCs define. Those registrations are intended to be updated by including them in revisions of the individual RFCs that define the payload formats.

The registrations follow the updated template format and procedures in RFC 4288 and RFC 4855. The update makes no technical changes in the registrations, and together with RFC 4855 this document obsoletes RFC 3555. No new registrations are contained here; the existing registrations for the omitted types remain valid until updated elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC lists the names for the encodings that the RTP conferencing profile uses. The names and the parameters attached to them are the same as before; only the format of the registration and the place it lives have changed.

sections.title: Registry Nomenclature
sections.content:
Because the media types registry is now generalized, as specified in RFC 4288, some names in the registry have to change. In the registry title "RTP Payload Format MIME types" and in the introductory text, "MIME" should be changed to "media". "MIME" should be deleted from the table headings, leaving just "media type" and "subtype".

The registrations listed in this document are updated to conform to the revised registration format, so the reference for these media types changes from RFC 3555 to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry used to be called a MIME registry. Since the registry now covers media types in general, the label changes to "media type" and the word MIME is dropped from the table headings.

sections.title: The Registered Media Types
sections.content:
Section 2 registers the RTP payload formats of RFC 3551 as media types. The audio subtypes are DVI4, G722, G723, G726-16, G726-24, G726-32, G726-40, G728, G729, G729D, G729E, GSM, GSM-EFR, L8, L16, LPC, PCMA, PCMU and VDVI. The video subtype is nv, which has no required or optional parameters.

Each registration states the encoding considerations, the security considerations, the interoperability considerations, the published specification, the applications that use the media type, the intended usage and the restrictions on usage. For the audio types the encoding considerations say the media type is framed binary data, as described in Section 4.8 of RFC 4288. Their restrictions on usage say that the media type depends on RTP framing and is therefore only defined for transfer via RTP, as given in RFC 3550, and that transfer within other framing protocols is not defined at this time. The intended usage is COMMON, and the change controller is the IETF Audio/Video Transport working group delegated from the IESG.

Media type audio/L16 was initially registered by RFC 2586 for transports other than RTP. That registration is incorporated here and augmented with additional information for RTP transport.
sections.plainLanguage: Each name gets the same set of notes: how the data is encoded, what it is used for, who looks after it, and where it may be carried. Nearly all of them are only defined for RTP, because the format depends on RTP framing.

sections.title: Audio Parameters
sections.content:
For most audio payload formats the RTP timestamp clock rate is equal to the sampling rate. Some payload formats operate only at one fixed sampling rate, while others are adjustable.

Five audio types require a rate parameter: audio/DVI4, audio/L8, audio/L16, audio/PCMA and audio/PCMU. For DVI4, PCMA and PCMU the rate is the RTP timestamp clock rate, which equals the sampling rate, and the typical rate is 8000, though other rates may be specified. For L8 the rate is the RTP timestamp clock rate, and for L16 it is the number of samples per second, which for RTP indicates the RTP timestamp clock rate and equals the sample rate.

The audio types also include the optional parameters ptime, which specifies the recommended length of time in milliseconds represented by the media in a packet, and maxptime, which specifies the maximum amount of media that can be encapsulated in each packet, also expressed in milliseconds. Both are defined in the Session Description Protocol, RFC 4566.

Some types add parameters of their own. audio/G723 has bitrate, the data rate in kb/s used or preferred for the audio bit stream, with permissible values 5.3 or 6.3, and if it is unspecified the bitrate may change from frame to frame as indicated inband. It also has annexa, which indicates that Annex A voice activity detection is used or preferred, with permissible values "yes" and "no" and "yes" implied if the parameter is omitted. The channels parameter, which says how many audio streams are interleaved and defaults to 1, with stereo being 2, appears on L8, L16, PCMA and PCMU, and interleaving takes place between individual one-byte samples for L8, PCMA and PCMU and between individual two-byte samples for L16.
sections.plainLanguage: The rate parameter says how many samples per second the audio has, and it is also the clock the receiver uses for the packet timestamps. Two more optional parameters, ptime and maxptime, say how much audio should be in one packet and how much is the most that may be put in one. Some codecs add a preferred bit rate or a switch for voice activity detection.

sections.title: The audio/L16 Registration
sections.content:
The registration of audio/L16 shows what a full entry looks like, because it is the one type that also carries parameters for transport other than RTP.

The required parameter is rate, the number of samples per second. For non-RTP transport the permissible values are 8000, 11025, 16000, 22050, 24000, 32000, 44100 and 48000 samples per second. For RTP transport other values are permissible, but those values are RECOMMENDED, and the rate parameter indicates the RTP timestamp clock rate, which equals the sample rate.

Three optional parameters are defined. channels says how many audio streams are interleaved, defaults to 1, and for L16 the interleaving takes place between individual two-byte samples. emphasis says what analog preemphasis was applied to the signal before quantization; the only value defined here is emphasis=50-15, indicating the 50/15 microsecond preemphasis used with Compact Discs, and the parameter MUST be omitted if no analog preemphasis was applied. It is a stream property parameter and not a receiver configuration parameter, so if parameters are negotiated it may not be possible for the sender to comply with a receiver request for a particular setting. channel-order specifies the sample interleaving order for multiple-channel audio streams, with values such as DV.LRLsRs, DV.LRCS and DV.LmixRmixTWoQ1Q2; only a subset of these is specified for use with 20-bit linear encoding in the DV video specification, and the parameter MUST be omitted when the AIFF-C channel order convention of RFC 3551 is in use.

The encoding considerations note that audio data is binary data and must be encoded for non-binary transport, for which Base64 is suitable for email, and that audio data does not compress easily using lossless compression. The type is compatible with the encoding used in the WAV and Apple AIFF union types, and with the public domain "sox" and "rateconv" programs. The published specification is RFC 2586 for non-RTP transports and RFC 3551 for RTP, and the file extensions are WAV and L16 with the Macintosh file type code AIFF.
sections.plainLanguage: L16 is uncompressed linear audio, so it needs to say how fast the samples come. For email and other file transfers only a fixed list of speeds is allowed, while over RTP any speed is allowed but the usual ones are recommended. It can also say how many channels are interleaved, what preemphasis was applied, and in what order the channels are laid out.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3555
sections.content:
RFC 3555 is obsoleted by the combination of RFC 4855 and this document. RFC 4855 retains the specification of procedures and requirements from RFC 3555, while the media type registrations from RFC 3555 were extracted into this document. The registrations for RTP payload formats that are referenced in RFC 3551 but defined in other RFCs have been elided, because those registrations are intended to be updated by including them in revisions of the individual RFCs defining the payload formats.

The registrations in this document have been updated to conform to the revised media type registration procedures in RFC 4288 and RFC 4855. Whereas RFC 3555 required the encoding considerations to specify transfer via RTP, that is now specified under restrictions on usage. The encoding considerations now warn that these types are framed binary data. The change controller is also now identified according to current conventions. The optional parameter "channels" was clarified for the audio subtypes L8, PCMA and PCMU. Finally, reference [9], which was missing from RFC 3555, has been corrected.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 3555 did two jobs: it described how the media types should be registered, and it held the registrations themselves. The two jobs are now split between RFC 4855 and this RFC. The registrations themselves did not change in substance, only in how they are written down.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document specifies media type registrations for the transfer of several compressed audio and video data encodings via RTP, so implementations using these media types are subject to the security considerations discussed in the RTP specification.

None of these media types carries active content that could impose malicious side effects on the receiver. The content consists solely of compressed audio or video data to be decoded and presented as sound or images. However, several audio and video encodings are well suited to hiding data using steganography.

A potential denial-of-service threat exists for encodings that use compression techniques with a non-uniform receiver-end computational load, because an attacker can inject pathological datagrams that are complex to decode and overload the receiver. None of the encodings registered here has an expansion factor greater than about 20, and all are considered relatively simple by modern standards; some are implemented on handheld devices and most were implemented on general-purpose computers ten years ago. As with any IP-based protocol, a receiver may also be overloaded simply by the receipt of too many packets, wanted or unwanted, and network-layer authentication MAY be used to discard packets from undesired sources, although the processing cost of the authentication itself may be too high.

RTP may be sent by IP multicast, which gives a sender no direct way to know who receives the data and therefore offers no measure of privacy. The RFC notes that users may be more sensitive to privacy concerns with audio and video communication than with more traditional forms of network communication, and that using the security mechanisms of RTP to provide confidentiality and integrity of the data is therefore important. Because the data compression used with these media types is applied end to end, encryption may be performed after compression, so there is no conflict between the two operations.
sections.plainLanguage: None of these encodings can run code on the receiver, but a compressed picture or sound can carry a hidden message. The other risk is that a carefully crafted packet is expensive to decode and slows the receiver down. Because the data is compressed end to end, encryption can be applied after compression, so the two do not get in each other's way.

viz.caption: THE MEDIA TYPES REGISTERED BY RFC 4856 AND THE PARAMETERS EACH ONE TAKES
THE PARAMETERS THE AUDIO TYPES USE

items.title: rate
items.text: The sampling rate, which for most audio types is also the RTP timestamp clock rate.

items.title: channels
items.text: How many audio streams are interleaved. Defaults to 1; stereo would be 2.

items.title: ptime
items.text: The recommended length of media in a packet, in milliseconds.

items.title: maxptime
items.text: The most media that may be put in one packet, in milliseconds.

items.title: bitrate
items.text: The data rate in kb/s used or preferred for the bit stream. G723 allows 5.3 or 6.3.

items.title: annexa
items.text: Whether Annex A voice activity detection is used or preferred. Values are yes and no.

items.title: emphasis
items.text: The analog preemphasis applied before quantization. Only 50-15 is defined.

items.title: channel-order
items.text: The sample interleaving order for multiple-channel audio, such as DV.LRLsRs.
